introduction.p: A separable differential equation has the form y\prime=g(t)h(y). On intervals where h(y)\ne0, divide by h(y) and integrate to obtain an implicit relation between t and y. Check the zeros of h separately, since they may give equilibrium solutions lost by division.

note.p: When you divide by an expression involving y, separately check the values of y that make that expression zero. They often give equilibrium solutions.

exercise.title: Why can dividing by an expression involving y lose solutions?

hint.p: Values that make the divided expression zero are candidates for equilibrium solutions. Check them separately before discarding them.

statement.p: Equations of the form Q'=-k(Q-Q_{\text{eq}}) appear for temperature, salt in a tank, and other adjustment models. In your own words, why does the quantity approach equilibrium exponentially, and why does it typically never reach that equilibrium in finite time?

subsection.title: Implicit solutions
subsection.p: Separation does not always lead to a clean formula
Sometimes the best answer is an equation that x and y satisfy together. Such an answer is called an implicit solution.

This equation is a perfectly meaningful solution. It tells us which points (x,y) lie on the solution curve.
We can also check it without solving for y. Differentiate both sides with respect to x:
So the implicit equation really does describe a solution of the differential equation.

note.title: Implicit solution
note.p: An implicit solution of a differential equation is an equation involving x and y whose differentiable branches satisfy the differential equation.
An explicit solution gives y directly as a function of x. An implicit solution may leave x and y tied together.

paragraphs.title: Domains still matter
paragraphs.p: Solving a differential equation is not just manipulating symbols until a formula appears. A solution must live on an interval where the function is differentiable and the equation makes sense.
A formula without a domain is not yet a complete solution.

note.title: What separable equations give us
note.p: Separation turns some differential equations into integral problems. It connects this chapter back to the Fundamental Theorem:

p.em: a law for a derivative \Longrightarrow an integral relation \Longrightarrow a solution curve.

paragraphs.p: The next separable model has two equilibrium solutions instead of one. It grows almost exponentially at first, slows as it approaches a limit, and has a characteristic slow--fast--slow shape.
That model is the logistic equation.

exercise.title: When is an implicit equation a legitimate solution?

statement.p: Separation may produce a relation such as y+y^3/3=x^2/2 instead of a formula y=f(x). In your own words, why can that still be a solution, and why is a formula without a domain still incomplete?

hint.p: Differentiating the implicit relation can recover the differential equation. A solution must live on an interval where the function is differentiable and the original equation makes sense.
